work_packages.name: An agent writes a game's scenes, phases and rules in plain Rust against one crate, in the order they run, and proves them in an ordinary test with no window
work_packages.quality_bar: Game code that reads as plainly as Bevy's `breakout` example with less ceremony: a scene function reads top to bottom as one tick, and no line names engine plumbing. Compiler and startup messages as useful as Rust's own, each naming the object, the cause and the next step. Correctness held as `SIM-2D` holds it: one trace, one digest. The reference for how game code reads is the design's worked examples, which the owner approves.

items.statement: Written order, and what a rule sees, in a game with no window built from `thrum` alone and stepped through `game.test()`. Build this item first: it rests on the engine applying a rule's structural edits when the rule ends, inside the tick's one transaction. (1) The entries of a scene function run once a tick in the order written, across `scene.rules` blocks and `scene.phase` blocks, and a phase block's rules run only while that is the scene's phase. (2) A rule reads what earlier rules of the same tick wrote to components and resources. (3) `spawn` returns the new entity's handle at once. The entity is visited by no query of the rule that spawned it and by the queries of every later rule of the same tick, and a later rule given that handle finds it alive with the components it was spawned with. An entity a rule despawns is still visited for the rest of that rule and by no later rule. A component inserted or removed is seen from the next rule on. (4) `despawn` returns true for the call that despawns an entity, and false for a second call in the same rule and for any later call. (5) A query visits entities in the order they were spawned, on every run, and its `With` and `Without` filters select as written. `pair_mut(a, b)` gives both items for two different entities the query matches, so a rule reads one and writes the other in one pass, and gives nothing when the two are the same entity or one is gone. `Single` gives the one match, and refuses the tick with none and with two. (6) An event a rule sends is read by later rules of that tick and by none in the next. (7) `rule.every(d)` runs first at the end of the first interval and once each interval after. A rule written in a phase's block counts on that phase's clock, so its count starts again each time the phase is entered. Any other rule counts from when the scene was entered, and goes on counting through a change of phase. A rule or group under `when` runs only in ticks where its condition holds. (8) `par_each` leaves the world as the serial loop does. (9) A component is known to the world, with no list written by the game, when the signature of a listed function names it, and a component that only a spawned tuple holds is known once the game says `Game::component::<T>()`. (10) A struct that derives `Params` and holds a `Query`, a `ResMut` and an `Emit` is taken by two rules as one parameter, and each rule reads, writes and sends through it as it would through the three. (11) `game.run(rule)` runs a rule function once between ticks, and what it did has landed when the call returns. Guard: CPU tests on worlds of a few entities, in `./dev check`.

Scenes, phases and time, in a game started with `test()` and stepped. (1) The game starts in the first scene listed, with its default value, and `test_in` starts in a given one. (2) A change of scene lands when the tick ends, in this order: the phase's exit functions, the scene's exit functions, the scene's entities despawned, scene resources set to the values they were registered with, the new scene's enter functions in the order written, the first phase's enter functions. Game resources keep their values. The next tick's first rule sees all of it, and reads the scene's value as `Res<S>` with the fields it was entered with. `restart()` enters the running scene again with the same value. (3) A change of phase lands when the tick ends, the old phase's exit functions before the new one's enter functions, and the tick's remaining rules run in the old phase. Going to the phase the scene is in leaves and enters it. `lasts(d).then(p)` changes phase at the tick `d` after entry, and `lasts` given a read-only function lasts the time that function returns when the phase is entered. The phase's clock is set before its enter functions run. In a phase two seconds long, both where `lasts` was given the time and where it was given a function that returns it, an enter function of the phase reads `phase.time()` as nothing and `phase.clock().left()` as two seconds, which is what the harness reads before the next tick. A function given to `lasts` reads a resource as an exit function of the phase being left wrote it, and as an enter function of the scene being entered wrote it, and a write to that resource by the new phase's own enter function does not change the length. `lasts(d).then_run(rule)` runs that rule once, at the tick `d` after entry and after every other rule of that tick: a `scenes.go_to` it makes lands when that tick ends, and where it asks for nothing the phase goes on and the rule does not run again. A rule of the tick the time is up reads the clock's `left()` as zero, and the harness reads it as `None` once that tick has ended with the phase going on. `phase.time()` is the time since entry, read from the phase's count of ticks: at 60 Hz, in a phase that `lasts(seconds(1))`, a rule's `phase.time() >= seconds(1)` first holds in the tick the `lasts` runs out. (4) A tick makes one transition at most, and the first request stands whichever kind it is. In each of these four pairs, made in this order in one tick, the first lands, the second returns false and nothing of the second happens: two `scenes.go_to`; two `PhaseMut::go_to`; a `PhaseMut::go_to` then a `scenes.go_to`; a `scenes.go_to` then a `PhaseMut::go_to`. In the tick a `lasts` runs out, a rule's `PhaseMut::go_to` to another phase lands and the `lasts` does not. (5) A request made while a transition lands. A `scenes.go_to` made by a phase's enter function, and one made by an exit function of a scene or of a phase, is the next tick's first request: that tick's rules run once, a rule's own request in it returns false, and the held one lands when that tick ends. A `PhaseMut::go_to` is held the same way where its scene is the one running once the landing ends: made by an enter function of the scene being entered, and by a phase's exit function during a change of phase. Made by an exit function of a scene that is being left, both for another scene that has no phases and by a `restart`, it returns false and no phase changes, and in the next tick a rule's `scenes.go_to` returns true and lands. (6) A scene given to `Game::scene` as a tuple of functions, or built with `scene.add`, is one scene whose entries run in the order those functions wrote them. (7) `Timer`: `running` is true from `start` until the tick its wait ends and `finished` from then on; both are false for `Timer::IDLE` and after `clear`. Half-way through a wait of two seconds `left` is one second and `fraction` is one half, and `fraction` is one from the tick the wait ends. `Cooldown::take` is true at once from `Cooldown::READY`, then once in each `every`, and a changed `every` applies from the next take. Between two takes `left` and `fraction` say how far the wait has run, with `fraction` one when it is ready, and `Cooldown::ready_after(tick, wait)` is first ready `wait` after that tick. (8) A scene resumed into a phase with its clock. `Phase::clock()` gives the running phase's clock as a value a resource and a scene's field hold. `PhaseMut::resume(p, clock)`, called by an enter function of a scene as that scene is entered, starts the scene in phase `p` with that clock: no enter function of any phase runs, a function given to `p`'s `lasts` is not asked, and leaving `p` runs its exit functions. Called by a rule, or by a phase's enter function, `resume` returns false and changes nothing. `resume` restores nothing else: `Tick::in_scene()`, and a rule under `every` outside any phase block, count from the new entry. The resumed phase carries on tick for tick. In a game at 60 Hz whose phase `p` has a length and a rule under `every` in its block, set beside a run of the same game that was not interrupted, for the 120 ticks after the entry: `phase.time()`, `Tick::in_phase()` and the clock's `left()` read in the k-th tick after the entry what that run reads in the k-th tick after the clock was taken; the rule under `every` runs in the same ticks, counted the same way; and `p`'s time is up in the same tick. That holds for a clock taken at each of three moments: by an enter function of `p`, where the run's k-th tick is counted from `p`'s entry; by a rule, one tick in; and by the harness between two ticks. Five cases by name. At one tick a second, a rule that runs every five seconds in `p`'s block, with the clock taken four seconds in, runs in the first tick after the entry. At 60 Hz, with the clock taken one tick in, `phase.time() >= seconds(1)` first holds as many ticks after the entry as it does, in the run not interrupted, after the tick the clock was taken in. At 60 Hz, a clock made by hand as `PhaseClock::at(t).ending_in(l)`, from the `time()` and the `left()` that a clock taken one tick into a ten-second phase gave, resumes as that clock does. Where `p`'s length came from a `lasts` function that returned ten seconds on entry, and the clock was taken four seconds in, after the resource that function reads had changed to twenty, the resumed phase runs out six seconds later. At one tick a second, in a phase two seconds long whose clock an enter function of `p` took, both where `lasts` was given the time and where it was given a function: resumed, the scene is in the phase `then` names after two ticks and not after one, as the run not interrupted is, and with `then_run` in place of `then` the rule has run once after two ticks in both runs. What follows `p`'s length happens once and is never lost, in a phase one second long at one tick a second, by four clocks. The first is taken before the time is up: resumed with it, the `then_run` rule runs once, in the tick the time left runs out. The second is taken by a rule in the tick the time is up, before what follows has happened, and reads `left()` as zero. Resumed with it, the harness reads the phase's `left()` as zero straight after the entry, before any tick, with the rule not yet run; then where `p` says `then_run` the rule runs once, in the first tick after the entry and after that tick's other rules, and in none of the next ten ticks, and where `p` says `then(q)` the scene is in `q` when the first tick after the entry ends. The third is the clock the harness takes in that committed world, straight after the entry with the second and before any tick: it reads `left()` as zero, and a scene entered again with it has the `then_run` rule run once, in the first tick after that entry, and in none of the next ten. The fourth is taken by the harness straight after the tick in which the `then_run` rule ran and asked for nothing, and reads `left()` as `None`: resumed with it, the phase goes on and the rule runs in none of the next ten ticks. (9) All of the above give the same world after a rewind to a tick inside the run and a replay. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

A scripted run of a test game that spawns, despawns, writes components and resources, changes phase and scene and draws from `Random`: (1) gives one world digest at every tick when run twice, when rewound to a tick inside the run and replayed, and when the same game is built again from its scene functions; (2) has a digest that covers the whole world: changing one field of one component, changing one field of one resource, spawning one entity, despawning one entity, and being in another phase or another scene each give another digest; (3) a draw from `Random` is fixed by the seed, the game's tick, the name of the function that asks and how many times that function has already run inside that tick, and by nothing else. With two named functions, `loot` and `weather`, each of which takes `Random`, returns nothing, as a scheduled rule must, and records its first three draws in the world, where the test reads them: (a) each records the same three in a game built again, and after a rewind and a replay; (b) the two record different draws from each other, and each records other draws at another seed and at another tick; (c) at one seed and one tick number, `loot`, the one function and no wrapper of it, records the same three on its first run of the tick by each of these routes: a scene's `rules`, alone and inside a tuple; a phase block's `rules`; under `every`; under `when`; as a `then_run` rule; as an enter function of a scene; and `game.run`, in a game whose description lists `loot` nowhere. A function that takes `Random` and is the condition of a `when`, and one that is the function a `lasts` is given, each returns through `game.run` what it returned to the scene at that seed and tick number; (d) a function listed twice in one scene draws differently in its two runs of one tick, and the same pair again after a rewind and a replay; (e) `game.run(loot)` called twice between the same two ticks records the same three; (f) a call made on a tick that is then discarded changes no later draw. `omen` is a third named function, which takes `Random`, writes nothing and returns its first draw. In a game stepped one tick, given `game.run(omen)` at that tick and then rewound that one tick, the rewind succeeds, the digest is what it was before the step, and `game.run(loot)` records what it records in a game where none of the three happened; (g) a closure that takes `Random`, and a function pointer that does, as an entry of an array of function pointers is, are each refused, as the error `test()` returns where a scene lists it and as the error `game.run` returns where it is passed there, with a message that carries a stable code and names the callable and the next step, which is to write a named function, and the world is unchanged. The same closure, and the same pointer, with no `Random` runs by both routes, in a game with no `rules` module; (h) two functions that take `Random`, declared under one name in two blocks of one function's body, are refused as a pair, with a message that carries a stable code and names the path they share and the next step, which is to give one of them another name. A game whose two scenes each list one of them is refused as the error `test()` returns, with no tick stepped and neither function run. In a game that lists the first, and in a game that lists neither where the test has already given the first to `game.run`, `game.run` of the second returns that error and the world is unchanged. The same pair with no `Random` in either starts and steps; (i) at seed 17 and the first tick, `loot` records the same three draws in two games: one whose scene lists it in `rules`, and one whose description lists it nowhere, where the test gives it to `game.run`. The tests hold those three numbers as literals, for each game, and pass in a debug build and in a release build; (4) a rule that returns an error refuses its tick, in a tick where earlier rules had already written a component, written a resource, spawned an entity that a later rule then visited, and despawned one: afterwards every component value, resource value and entity count read back through the harness is what it was before the tick, the error names the rule and the tick, and the next `step()` runs as if the refused tick had not been tried; (5) on the Mac, a rule that panics is reported the same way, with the same values read back. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`, which hold (i)'s literals. Record: the same tests passing in a release build, run once by this item's check.
items.check: cargo test --locked --offline -p thrum --test it replay:: && cargo test --locked --offline --release -p thrum --test it replay::

items.statement: Each of these mistakes is refused with a message that carries its stable code and names the object, the cause and the next step, and leaves the world unchanged where a world exists. At compile time: a component, a resource, an event or a scene's field that is a `Vec`, a `String`, a reference, a raw float or `usize`; a first scene whose type has no default. At startup, as the error `test()` returns, with no tick stepped: a rule that reads a resource nothing provides; a rule with one `Query` that names a component twice, once with `&mut`, as `Query<(&mut Health, &Health)>` does, in a game with no entity, whose message names the rule, the parameter and the component; a rule two of whose accesses reach one resource, one of them writing it, in each of three cases (`ResMut<Ledger>` beside `Res<Ledger>`; a struct that derives `Params` and holds `ResMut<Ledger>`, beside `Res<Ledger>`; two such structs that each hold `ResMut<Ledger>`), whose message names the rule, both parameters and the resource; a rule that takes `Entities` twice; a scene that calls `phases` twice, whose message names the scene. While running, each refusing its tick: a spawn of a component that no signature names and the game has not declared, whose message names the rule, the component and `Game::component`; an entity that two parameters of one rule both match on a component one of them writes, in each of four cases (both parameters write it; one writes it and the other reads it; an entity that matched one of them comes to match both when an earlier rule inserts a component; one of the two parameters is a field of a struct that derives `Params`), whose message names the rule, both parameters, the component and the entity; `Single` with none and with two; `go_to` a scene the game was not given; a spawn past the world's size; a rule that returns an error. Three games start and step with no complaint: one with two parameters of one rule that name the same component, both writing it and one writing it while the other reads it, where no entity matches both, with no `Without`; one with a rule that takes `Res<Ledger>` twice, once inside a struct that derives `Params`; and one whose scenes have no camera, no binding and no frame function. The tests hold each message's code, object, cause and next step by its text. Guard: in `./dev check`.

No type of another crate reaches a game through `thrum`. Each type in a public signature of `thrum` resolves to a type defined in `thrum` or its derive crate, to a type of Rust's own from `core`, `alloc` or `std`, or to a generic parameter, which stands for the game's own type. A type defined in any other crate is refused wherever it stands in a public function, method, field, trait bound, associated type, re-export or alias, as a type argument of another type included, judged on the type as it resolves and not on how the item spells it. The surface check has seven controls, scratch crates it is run on. It fails each of these five, naming the item and the foreign type: a public method that returns an engine type brought in by a private `use`; a public alias of an engine type; a public re-export of one; a public struct with a public field of one; a public method that returns an `Option` of one. It passes each of these two: a public method that returns an `Option` of the crate's own type, as `Option<Entity>` is; a public generic method that returns `&T`, as `Content<T>::get` does. Every public item of `thrum` has a doc comment with an example, and every example runs as a doc test. A package that names `thrum` with default features off builds alone and has no renderer, window, GPU, network or platform crate in its dependency closure. `thrum` and any crate it is built from are registered in `.config/architecture.toml`. Guard: the surface check, its controls and the doc tests run in `./dev check` from this landing, so every later work package's additions are held to them.
items.check: python3 scripts/sdk_surface.py check && python3 scripts/sdk_surface.py controls && cargo test --locked --offline -p thrum --doc

items.statement: The SDK is a layer over the engine's simulation and adds no second one.
items.ask: Read `thrum` and the tests' games. 1. Is world state held anywhere but `thrum-core`'s registered simulation: is there a second store, clock or undo? Which scene and phase run are world state there too? Is a draw from `Random` a function of the seed, the game's tick, the function's name and its count of runs inside that tick alone, and so the same in every build of the same sources by one version of the compiler, whatever the profile, the features or the target: does any part of a draw's key come from an address, a Rust type ID, the order in which functions were registered or called, a table that fills as they are, or a hasher whose output may differ between builds? Is a Rust type compared only to tell whether two functions of one name are one function? Does a run outside a tick, as `game.run` makes, leave the count as it was? Is a phase's clock kept as two counts of ticks, set before the phase's enter functions run, with every time read from a count and none made by adding two times? 2. Are a rule's structural edits applied when the rule ends inside the tick's one transaction, so that a refused tick undoes them with everything else, and does a rule that staged none pay nothing for the barrier? 3. Is the loop over entities inside a rule monomorphised for that rule's parameters, with no dynamic call and no allocation for each entity, and no allocation for each tick once warm? One call for each rule each tick through the engine's registered callback is as designed. 4. Does a component's schema identity come from its name and fields, and never from a Rust type ID? 5. Are the changes made in `thrum-core` additions only, with its existing tests unedited and passing? 6. Does any test's game name a crate other than `thrum`, or a schema number, permit, executor, page or device?

items.statement: Game code for the headless subset is written as the design's worked examples write it. Every difference between the built API and the parts of the examples that the design's section "What WP1 compiles" lists is a line in the module's log, and none is a change of shape as the design's section "What a builder may change" defines one.
items.ask: Set the tests' games beside the parts of the worked examples that the design's section "What WP1 compiles" lists: from example A, `Score`, `drop_rocks` with its cadence, `fall`, and `Play` and `GameOver` joined by `go_to` with the score as the scene's field; from example E, `Run`, `Stage`, its three phase blocks with their lengths, `next_wave`, `enemies_die`, `heroes_fall` and `clear_enemies`. Set the rule parameters beside these entries of the design's reference, group R3, and the `Params` derive in R1: `Query`, `Single`, `Res` and `ResMut`, `Entities`, `Events` and `Emit`, `Tick`, `Random`, `Scenes`, `Phase` and `PhaseMut`, and a struct that derives `Params`. Leave out what that section gives to later work packages. List each difference in how a game maker writes the same thing. Is each one in the log as a spelling? Is any a change of shape? A change of shape that is not the owner's own fails this item.

findings.name: Distinct 64-bit game seeds produce identical draw streams
findings.different: The named function now draws identically across debug and release. The new failure occurs within either build when different seeds collapse to the same generator key.

findings.name: Setting a component to its current value discards rewind history

work_packages.name: A game names a reusable thing, spawns it and variants of it, attaches one thing to another and takes a thing out of play
work_packages.quality_bar: Reuse as plain as Unity's prefab variants and Godot's scenes, in Rust with no editor: a variant is a base and a difference, and a child is one line. The reference for how game code reads is the design's worked examples E and G, which the owner approves.

items.statement: Prefabs, in a game with no window started with `test()` and stepped. (1) A prefab named in a `prefabs!` block and defined with `Game::prefab` is spawned at a place with `.at` and `.at_point`, with the components of its definition. (2) `.with(c)` on a definition and on a spawn replaces the component of that type or adds it, and `.tweak` changes one field and leaves the others. (3) A variant is its base with its changes: every component the variant did not change has the base's value, and that still holds when the base is defined after the variant. (4) A `Prefab<N>` is spawned with the `N` its spawn brings. (5) A child and a named part given in a definition are spawned with the entity, at their local places, and despawned with it. (6) A prefab's components are known to the world with no other line. (7) A test spawns a prefab with `game.spawn` and gets its entity. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

Children, parts and disabling, in a game started with `test()` and stepped. In (1) and (2) every number composes exactly: parents and children stand at whole-number positions, and parents are turned by quarter turns and scaled by two. (1) `attach(child).to(parent)` with `keep_world` leaves the child's place in the world bit for bit as it was, and with `keep_local(pose)` puts it at that local place. `detach` with `keep_world` leaves it bit for bit where it stood, and `detach(child).at(pose)` leaves it with no parent at that place in the world. (2) `world2d` and `world3d` give a child's place through two levels of such parents. (3) `parent` and `children` answer, the children in the order they were attached, and `part` reaches a named part. (4) Despawning a parent despawns its children and theirs. (5) Attaching, detaching and disabling land when the rule ends, as a spawn does. A rule attaches the entity it has just spawned, by the handle `spawn` returned, under another entity, and a spawn that says `.under(parent)` is that parent's child: each is among that parent's `children` from the next rule on. (6) A disabled entity and its children keep their components. Until they are enabled, an ordinary query, which is one with neither the `Disabled` nor the `WithDisabled` filter, visits none of them, and a query with the `Disabled` filter visits them and no enabled entity. From the rule after `enable` an ordinary query visits them as before. So a rule finds what it disabled and reads a `Timer` on it. `disable` returns true for the call that disables an entity and false for a second call, and `enable` the same. (7) A child at x = 1/10, made by dividing one by ten, attached with `keep_world` under a parent at x = 10 scaled by two, a place no local transform recomposes bit for bit, is attached and not refused, and stands within one part in 2^17 of ten units of where it stood. (8) All of it gives the same world after a rewind and a replay, and the digest changes when a parent changes. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

Each of these mistakes is refused with a message that carries its stable code and names the object, the cause and the next step. At compile time: a spawn of a `Prefab<N>` that does not bring its `N`. At startup, as the error `test()` returns, with no tick stepped: a name declared in a `prefabs!` block that has no definition, in each of four cases (only a rule's body spawns it, in a branch a run would first reach at its hundredth tick, from a block another of whose names the game defines; the same from a block of its own, none of whose names the game's description defines or names; a definition uses it as a base; a definition uses it as a child or a part), whose message names the prefab, its block and `Game::prefab`; a prefab that two parameters of one rule both match on a component one of them writes, whose message names the rule, the parameters, the component and the prefab. While running, each refusing its tick with the world unchanged: `part` on an entity whose prefab has no such part; an attachment that would make a cycle; `keep_world` under a parent whose scale is zero and under one whose scale is below 1/10,000, after each of which the child's parent, local place and place in the world read back as they were. The tests hold each message's code, object, cause and next step by its text. Guard: in `./dev check`.
Prefabs and the tree cost nothing where they are not used, `keep_world` is held to its bound on every call, and both read as the design's examples do.
items.ask: 1. Is a prefab, with its variants, resolved once when the game starts, so that a spawn copies a prepared set of components with no lookup by name and no allocation? 2. Does an entity with no parent and no child hold or pay for anything of the tree, in a query and in the digest's work? 3. Is the place a `keep_world` recomposes compared with where the child stood on every call, and the attachment refused past the design's bound, with the residual and the bound in the error? 4. Set the tests' games beside example E's `prefabs` function, its spawns of `BAT`, `ELITE_BAT`, `GEM` and `SHOT`, and example G's `take_or_set_down`. Is each difference in the log as a spelling, and is none a change of shape as the design's section "What a builder may change" defines one?

items.statement: Owning and finding, in a game with no window started with `test()` and stepped. (1) A spawn brings children chosen where it is made. A prefab whose definition has one child, spawned with `.child(..)` said twice, lands with three children: the definition's first and then the two the spawn gave, in that order among `children`, each at its local place and with the component its own spawn gave it, and each despawned with the entity. The handle `spawn` returned is their parent's. (2) A spawn that says `.disabled()` lands disabled, with its children: no query without a filter for it visits it in any later rule, a query with the `Disabled` filter does, and `enable` returns true for it. (3) `Query::under(parent)` visits the children of `parent` that the query matches, in the order they were attached, and reads and writes them as the query does. It visits no grandchild, no child of another parent and no entity with no parent, and nothing for a parent with no children or one that is gone. A named part is visited as any child is. A child a rule attached or spawned under the parent is visited from the next rule on. (4) A query with the `WithDisabled` filter visits the entities it matches whether they are disabled or not, each once, in the order they were spawned. A tuple of filters selects what every one of them selects: `(With<A>, Disabled)` visits the disabled entities that have `A` and no others. (5) `Option<&T>` in a query's item is `Some` for an entity that has `T` and `None` for one that has not, and the query visits both. `Option<&mut T>` writes where it is `Some`, and is a write of `T` to the access check: a rule that takes such a query beside a `Query<&T>` that reaches the same entity is refused as any two conflicting parameters are. (6) All of it gives the same world after a rewind to a tick inside the run and a replay. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

work_packages.name: A crowd of 10,000 written on the SDK, steered by four players, steps identically on the Mac, in Chrome and on the iPhone simulator, and costs what the hand-written crowd does
work_packages.quality_bar: Determinism as Factorio holds it: the same inputs give the same world on every machine, checked by digest. Speed as the engine's own reference crowd: the layer is not what a tick is spent on. A first character that is steered as directly as Godot's first-game player. Rules that read as example E of the design does.

items.statement:
Players, action maps and a controlled character, in a game started with `test()` and stepped. Action maps: a rule reads a player's map with `Inputs::of` as plain fields, and an `Axis` and a `Stick` multiply and compare as a `Num` and a `Vec2`. Buttons: `held` is true while the button is down; `pressed` is true in exactly one tick for a press, the first admitted after it; `released` is true in the tick the button is found up after being held; `presses` is how many times it went down since the last tick. With a player's frames lost through the harness: a frame repeated for a missing one gives no press and keeps what was held; a neutral frame releases what was held; frames that come back after a neutral one give no press when no press was made in the gap, and one press, read in one tick, when one was; two presses between two admitted frames give `presses == 2` in one tick. Players: `PlayerJoined` is read once for a player, at the tick they enter the game, and not again in a later scene; `PlayerLeft`, `PlayerAway` and `PlayerBack` are read at the tick of each; `Players` gives who is here in seat order, the host and each player's status, and has no method that changes the roster; a game stepped with no roster script has one player from the first tick. A `Player` value names one stay in a seat: after a player leaves and another person takes the same seat, the value kept from before reads `Gone` from `Players::status`, `None` from `PerPlayer::get` and no entity from `Query::of_player`, while the newcomer's own value reads theirs; `PlayerLeft` carries the leaver's name; and a `PerPlayer` value is back at its default once its seat's player has left. One character for each player. A scene's `players().spawn(..)` gives a character to each player already here when the scene is entered and to each who arrives later, so that with two players joined in a first scene, a second scene with such a line has two characters, a third player who joins later makes three, and no player ever has two; a spawn function is given `Joined` and read-only parameters; `Players::character(p)` and `Query::of_player(p)` give that character, and nothing for a player who has none; a character is despawned when its player leaves, stays under idle input while they are away, and follows `when_away` when that says otherwise; `PlayersMut::respawn` brings back one a rule despawned, and for a player whose character still lives despawns it and puts the new one in its place. Which entity is the character: a player has one at most and an entity is one player's at most, and the SDK's `Player` component is on a player's character and on no other entity. An entity that holds a player's `Player` value in a component of the game's own, as a drone would, is never given by `character` or `of_player` and never moved by the control function. `PlayersMut::possess(p, other)`, where `other` is alive, has the components the control function takes and is nobody's character, returns true, and from the next rule on `character(p)` and `of_player(p)` give `other`, `other` holds `p`'s `Player` component and the entity they had before holds none, the control function moves `other` with that player's input, and the entity they had before stays in the world where it stood. With two players who each have a character, `possess` of the second player's character for the first returns false: afterwards `character` gives each player the entity it gave before, each of the two entities holds the `Player` component it held, and in the next tick the control function moves each player's own character with that player's own input, the two steering different ways. `possess` of a player's own character, and of a despawned entity, returns false and changes nothing. The control function runs where its line is written among the scene's entries, once a tick for each player's character in seat order, with that character's components and that player's map, so two players steering different ways each move their own; `.during(phase)` runs it only in that phase, and a scene with two control lines, each `.during` another phase, moves the one character by the first function in the first phase and by the second in the second; alone it may also take `Res`, `Phase

` and `Emit`, and an event it sends is read by later rules of the tick. Seats and bots: a person who joins takes the lowest free seat; `PlayersMut::add_bot` takes the highest free seat, is announced as a player is and returns none when every seat is taken; input a rule sets with `BotInputs` before the control line is read by the control function in the same tick; a button a rule holds down in a bot's map for three ticks and then lets go reads `pressed` in the first of them, `held` in all three and `released` in the tick after; a bot's character is spawned, moved and despawned as a person's is; a person who joins when bots hold every free seat takes the lowest seat a bot holds, and in that tick `PlayerLeft` is read for the bot, its character is despawned, `PlayerJoined` is read for the person, the person has one new character and no seat has two; a person who joins when people hold every seat is refused, the harness's `join()` returning the full error with no event read, no character spawned and no seat changed. All of it gives the same world after a rewind to a tick inside the run and a replay. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

`Space2d` over entities with a `Collider2d`. (1) `touching`, `within`, `in_rect`, `nearest` and `sweep_circle` find the same set of entities `thrum-sim2d`'s queries find for the same circles, and exactly the overlapping ones for rectangles and capsules, with offsets, on the layer asked, less any entity named by `except`. The order they come in is the SDK's own, whatever order the index gives: nearest first with ties by spawn order, and for `sweep_circle` earliest contact first with ties by spawn order. (2) `.on(LAYER)` answers from that layer's colliders alone: `nearest` on one layer returns that layer's nearest collider when colliders of another layer stand nearer, with a radius and without one. A query with no `.on` returns every layer's answer merged in the same order. (3) A query answers from where colliders are when its rule starts: it finds an entity the previous rule spawned or moved where it now is, and does not find one the previous rule despawned. `at_tick_start()` answers from where colliders stood when the tick began. (4) `motion_of(entity).sweep()` reports the earliest contact along the path the entity took this tick against the paths the others took: a body moved through another between two ticks is reported hit, one spawned this tick is swept from where it was spawned, and a tie goes to the earlier spawned. (5) A layer's index is built at most once after each rule that changed that layer and not at all in a tick that changed none, which a count the test reads shows. (6) A scene's cell size is part of its rule set. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

The numbers page holds, the profile's additions are exactly rounded and refuse what a rule may not reach, and nothing retained changed. Every row of the table in the design's section 8, Numbers, marked allowed compiles and gives the value written, and each row marked not allowed fails to compile or is refused by the check, as that row says. An integer converts as that table says: 16,777,216 exactly, and 16,777,217 to 16,777,216. `num`, `Vec2::lit` and `Seconds::lit` are usable in a `const`. `Angle` and its `sin`, `cos` and directions, turning a `Vec2` and a `Vec3`, and `Rot3` products have conformance vectors beside the profile's own. A child attached with `keep_world` under a parent turned by 37 degrees and scaled by 1.5, within 100 units of the origin, stands within 0.001 of a unit of where it stood. The profile's controls refuse, each with a message that names the reason, checked rules that read a file through `std::fs`, open a socket through `std::net`, start a process through `std::process` or read standard input, beside every refusal the profile already made. The reference crowd's retained digests are unchanged. Guard: the vectors, the profile check and its controls run in `./dev check`.
items.check: cargo test --locked --offline -p thrum --test it numbers:: && python3 scripts/sim2d_profile.py check && python3 scripts/sim2d_profile.py controls && cargo test --locked --offline -p crowd-2d --test retained_slice

items.statement: Each of these mistakes is refused with a message that carries its stable code and names the object, the cause and the next step. At compile time: a field of an action map with neither `#[bind]` nor `#[sent]`; a `LocalActions` map asked for by a rule; a field of world state that is a raw float, whose message names `Num`; a spawn function given to `players().spawn` that takes `PlayersMut`, `ResMut<T>` or `Entities`; a bare `Player` in a spawned tuple, given to `Entities::insert` and named by `Entities::remove`, and a `Query` that asks for `&mut Player`, each with a message that names a component of the game's own as where to keep one. At startup, as the error `test()` returns: action maps that do not fit an input frame, with the counts and the limit; a control function that takes `&mut T` and `&T` of one component of its character; a control function with a `Query` that reaches the character its line spawns, over a component either writes; a scene with two `players().spawn(..)` lines; a scene with two control lines that could run in the same phase, whose message names the scene and both lines. While running, each refusing its tick with the world unchanged: `PlayersMut::possess` of an entity that lacks a component the control function takes, after which the player's character reads back as the one it was; a player's character that comes to be reached by a `Query` of its own control function over a component either writes, in each of two cases (a rule inserts a component on the character; `PlayersMut::possess` gives the player an entity the query matches, after which the player's character reads back as the one it was), whose message names the function, the parameter, the component, the player and the entity. A control function that takes `&mut Transform2d` for its character beside a `Query<&Transform2d, With<Enemy>>` starts and steps with no complaint and no `Without`, and still does after `possess` gives the player another entity that is no enemy, which the function then moves. A game whose action set is a `Stick`, a `Heading` and four `Button`s fits the input frame and starts with no complaint. The tests hold each message's code, object, cause and next step by its text. Guard: in `./dev check`.

On the Mac, `crowd-sdk` gives the digests its retained trace holds, and its trace row carries these witnesses, each more than nothing: for each of the four players, how far their hero moved along the direction that player's script steers, the four scripts steering up, down, left and right; hits; deaths; respawns; the angle the turning body turned through; how many prefab names the SDK knew when the game started, before it read the game's description, which is every name `crowd-sdk` declares; and ticks a rule refused by returning an error at a scripted tick, after each of which the components and resources read back were what they were before it. `crowd-sdk` is a game under `examples/crowd-sdk` that names only `thrum`, with its rules in its `rules` module: four players' heroes moved by a control function on a `scene.players()` line, enemies that chase the nearest hero and keep apart with `par_each`, shots at the nearest enemy that hit by `motion_of(..).sweep()`, deaths that drop a pick-up collected in the same tick, respawns, and a body that turns by an `Angle` each tick, at 10,000 bodies. Record: the Mac arm of the three-target conformance run. A slice of the trace, with its witnesses, stays as a CPU test in `./dev check`.
items.check: python3 scripts/sim2d_conformance.py run --package crowd-sdk --target mac-metal && cargo test --locked --offline -p crowd-sdk --test it retained::

items.statement: In Chrome, `crowd-sdk` gives the digests its retained trace holds, with every witness WP2.5 names more than nothing. The conformance runner takes Chrome's lock itself around its browser run, so the item names none. Record: the Chrome arm of the three-target conformance run.

On the iPhone simulator, `crowd-sdk` gives the digests its retained trace holds, with every witness WP2.5 names more than nothing. Function only. The conformance runner takes the simulator for each of its turns itself, so the item names no lock. Record: the simulator arm of the three-target conformance run.

On the Mac, two release takes each of `crowd-sdk` and of the reference crowd at 10,000 bodies report the cost of a tick, of a rewind and of a replay, and the allocations of a warmed tick, side by side, with the build and the load on the machine. The takes of `crowd-sdk` are of the load WP2.5 describes: the record carries, counted over the measured ticks, each of the four players' hero movement, hits, deaths and respawns, each more than nothing, and how many times each layer's index was built in a tick, beside the reference's own witnesses for its takes. The record flags for investigation a `crowd-sdk` tick more than about 25% above the reference's, and any allocation in a warmed `crowd-sdk` tick. The check fails only on a missing measurement or a missing witness. The record also names the default number of entities a world holds and why. Record: SDK rule cost beside the hand-written reference, taken under load.
`crowd-sdk` reads as example E of the design does, and what the SDK added to the engine for it belongs to the engine's owners.
items.ask: 1. Read `crowd-sdk`'s rules beside example E. Does its scene function read top to bottom as one tick, and does each rule read as one thing the game does? Does the package hold a helper file that hides plumbing a game maker would have to write: registration, encoding, scheduling, index building? Count every file of the package as game lines. 2. Is each difference from the design's examples in the log as a spelling, and is none a change of shape? 3. Are the profile's additions in `thrum-core`'s profile and `thrum-sim2d`, with no platform maths call, and do the reference crowd's rules and retained traces stand unedited? 4. Does `Space2d` keep one `thrum-sim2d` index for each layer with its storage between ticks, and answer a query on a layer from that layer's index alone, so that an enemy's nearest-hero query looks at the heroes and not at the crowd? 5. Is the heroes' control function their whole movement step, writing the pose itself?

items.statement: A game outside the engine checkout, one package laid out as the design's templates are with its rules in `src/rules.rs` and reaching the engine by path, passes the engine's external game check and the check of its own rules, and its own test starts it with `test()`. The same game fails its own check, with a message that names the line and the violation, with each of these in its `rules` module: raw-float arithmetic; a file read; a call to a function defined elsewhere in the game; a constant under `#[cfg(feature = "..")]` for a feature the game's manifest declares and the check leaves off; a `cfg!(..)` in a rule's body. The same game, its `rules` module unchanged and still holding a rule `score`, fails its own check with a function named `rules` at the root of its crate, in whose body a second function `score` is declared, in each of three cases: the game lists both functions `score` as rules; it lists only the one declared in that body; and the root function is written by a macro of the game's own and the game lists neither. Each message names the root function, its line or the line that calls the macro, and the next step, which is to give it another name. The same game is refused at startup, as the error `test()` returns, with a message that names the function and the `rules` module, with each of these defined outside that module: a rule; a control function; a spawn function given to `scene.players().spawn(..)`; an enter function; a condition; a function given to a phase's `lasts`. It is refused at startup the same way with a rule listed as a function pointer, as an entry of an array of `fn` pointers is, to a function defined inside the module, with a message that names the pointer's type and the next step, which is to list the function by its name. A game that keeps its rules in a package of its own, marked in that package's manifest, passes the same way and fails the same way. So does a game that is one source file with its rules in a `mod rules { .. }` block of that file: it passes both checks, its own test starts it with `test()`, and it fails its own check with raw-float arithmetic in the block and is refused at startup with a rule defined outside the block. A game with no `rules` module, its rules written at the top of its one file, fails the check of its own rules with a message that names those rules and `mod rules { .. }`, while its own test still starts it with `test()` and steps it. The engine's check of its registered rule packages still passes throughout, and the external game check still refuses a game package that names an engine example and a path that leaves the game's folder for anything but the engine's crates. Guard: a test over scratch games outside the checkout, in `./dev check`.

A character arrives whole and a leaver's last values are read, in a game started with `test()` and stepped. (1) A spawn function given to `players().spawn(..)` returns a prefab at a place with a `.child(..)` chosen from `Joined` and from a resource. Each player's character appears with that child under it, in the landing that makes the character and with no other rule: for each of two players here when the scene is entered, and for a third who joins later. (2) `CharacterSpawned { player, character }` is read once for each character the scene's spawn makes, naming that player and that entity. For each player here as a scene is entered, every rule of that scene's first tick reads it, the first rule included. For a player who joins later it is read in the tick their character appears, and for `PlayersMut::respawn` by the rules after the one that called it, to the end of that tick. No rule of a later tick reads it. One is sent for a bot's character as for a person's, a second scene with a players' line sends one for each player again, and `PlayersMut::possess` sends none. (3) `PerPlayer::departed(p)`. In the tick a player leaves, every rule, one that reads `PlayerLeft` included, reads through `departed(p)` the value that player's seat held when they left, while `get(p)` reads `None`. Where a person takes a bot's seat in one tick, `departed(bot)` reads the bot's value, the person's own value reads the default, and a rule that then adds to the person's value leaves `departed(bot)` as it was. In the next tick `departed(p)` reads `None`. For a player who is here, and for one who left in an earlier tick, it reads `None`. (4) All of it gives the same world after a rewind to a tick inside the run and a replay. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

A hit says where the mover stood at first contact, how deep, what motion it had left and how fast the two were closing. Every case is `motion_of(entity).sweep()` over circles whose positions rules wrote, so each path is one straight line over the whole tick, unless it says `sweep_circle`. Two circles touch where the gap between them, or the depth of one in the other, is no more than the 2D contact tolerance of the design's section 7, which the reference states and which is no more than 1/65,536 of the larger of one unit and the largest coordinate or size of the two shapes. (1) Met on the way: a circle moved through a still circle between two ticks reports a `fraction` between zero and one; a `mover_position` on its path at that fraction, where a circle of the mover's radius touches the struck one; a `depth` of exactly zero; an `approach_speed` above zero; and a `remaining_motion` that added to `mover_position` is where the mover ended the tick. (2) The same against a body that also moved this tick, where the contact is found along both paths and `mover_position` is on the mover's own. (3) Begins touching: a circle of radius 1 whose path begins with its centre two units along an axis from the centre of another of radius 1 reports fraction zero, a `mover_position` where its path began, a `depth` of exactly zero and its whole path as `remaining_motion`. (4) Begins inside, along an axis: a circle of radius 1 whose path begins with its centre one unit along an axis from the centre of another of radius 1 reports fraction zero, a `mover_position` where its path began, a `depth` of exactly 1, a normal along the line between the centres toward the mover, and its whole path as `remaining_motion`. Set at `mover_position + normal * depth` its centre is exactly two units from the other's. (5) Begins inside, on the diagonal: with a circle of radius 1 at (0, 0) and a mover of radius 1 whose path begins at (1, 1), the hit reports fraction zero, a `mover_position` of (1, 1) and a `depth` within the tolerance of 2 less the square root of 2. A mover set at `mover_position + normal * depth`, worked out by a rule in its own numbers, touches the other, and its sweep from there reports that circle at fraction zero with a `depth` of exactly zero. (6) The hits of (3), (4) and (5) are reported with the same `fraction`, `mover_position`, `depth` and normal when the path leads away from the struck circle. (7) Closing and parting, for a hero that begins a tick touching the top of a watch. The hero rises one unit and the watch two: `approach_speed` is above zero. The hero rises one unit and the watch stands still: it is below zero, and its size is within one part in a thousand of one unit divided by the tick's length in seconds. Both rise one unit: it is zero. `remaining_motion.dot(normal)` is above zero in all three. (8) `sweep_circle(from, to, radius)` in each of the cases (1), (3) and (4): `mover_position` is the swept circle's centre at first contact, which met on the way stands the radius from the `point` touched, and `mover_position` plus `remaining_motion` is `to`. (9) A rule that sets a hero at the `mover_position` of its stomp and moves it on by the length of `remaining_motion`, upward, leaves it clear of what it struck in that same tick, with no second query. (10) Each gives the same values after a rewind and a replay. Guard: CPU tests on worlds of a few bodies, in `./dev check`.
